entities.summary:
Ma Shi (courtesy name Jingzhan, 敬瞻), an eminent figure of the early Ming dynasty, embodied the polymath ideal of the Chinese scholar-official through his distinguished careers as a landscape painter, court astronomer, and poet. Flourishing during the Xuande era (1425–1435), an epoch renowned for its imperial patronage of the arts and sciences, Ma Shi’s multifaceted talents placed him at the heart of the imperial court in Nanjing. Though his precise birth and death dates remain elusive, his contributions significantly enriched the cultural and scientific landscape of 15th-century China, reflecting the sophisticated intellectual environment of the period.

As a painter, Ma Shi was celebrated for his landscape works, which often blended the meticulous brushwork of the Northern Song tradition with the expressive qualities of the Southern Song masters, contributing to the distinct aesthetic of the early Ming imperial academy. His artistic output, though not extensively documented in surviving works, established a benchmark for court painters and influenced subsequent generations. Concurrently, his role as a court astronomer was equally vital, involving the observation of celestial phenomena and the maintenance of the imperial calendar, a critical function for legitimizing dynastic rule. He was instrumental in recording astronomical events, contributing to the precision of the Chinese calendrical system.
